title: AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?
text:
AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

AI has sped up how teams design and build, but quality assurance (QA) testing hasn’t kept pace, and the web may be getting less accessible. Drawing on new research, Andrew Chung explains what separates the teams whose accessibility efforts are keeping up, and how to embed human judgment into AI-enabled workflows without slowing delivery.

title: Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams
text:
Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

An AI feature can save users time on a task, only for them to spend it checking the results. This practical audit helps product teams decide where AI earns its place and what users need to verify its output.

title: Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible
text:
Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible

As LLM chat patterns become more widespread, making them accessible is essential to ensuring everyone can access the information, tools, and opportunities they offer. Drawing on his work improving these interfaces, Eric Bailey shares practical ways to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who rely on assistive technology.

title: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex
text:

Replacing JavaScript with a modern CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about. Gabriel Shoyombo explores what happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, sharing practical guidance to help you keep complexity in check during migration.

title: Lessons from 3D scanning St John’s Co-Cathedral
text:
Lessons from 3D scanning St John’s Co-Cathedral

Seven nights, 99,000 photographs and 25 billion triangles showed us where photogrammetry works and where gold, marble and fabric still beat it, as we reported at SIGGRAPH 2026.

Summary

Over seven nights of evening-only access, we digitised St John’s Co-Cathedral in Valletta, Malta, a UNESCO World Heritage site holding two Caravaggio paintings. The result is a photogrammetric reconstruction of 25 to 30 billion triangles, built from 99,000 photographs and 43 laser scans, alongside an experimental Gaussian splatting reconstruction of one chapel.

I served as the external technical expert for St John’s Co-Cathedral Foundation, leading this project. Andre Grima, Peter Pullicino and Matthew Pullicino from Stargate Studios Malta carried out the digitisation and production. Matthew Kenely from SeyTravel and Mark Bugeja from the University of Malta handled the documentation. This project was part-financed by The Melita Foundation.

7 nights · 99,000 photographs · 43 LiDAR scans · 2.18 TB processed · 3 months of processing · 25 to 30 billion triangles

The complete technical methodology, including the equipment specifications, accuracy metrics and processing pipeline, is documented in the peer-reviewed paper, Large-Scale Photogrammetric Documentation of St John’s Co-Cathedral: A Workflow for Cultural Heritage Preservation, presented at ACM SIGGRAPH 2026 Art Papers and available on The ACM Digital Library as Open Access (free) here: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3816089.

Once-in-a-generation opportunity

The year 2023 sounds like just another year in the 400+-year-old history of a cathedral, but it did, in fact, open a once-in-a-generation opportunity. The last pieces of the Perellos Tapestries had just returned to Malta after an extensive 16-year restoration process of the entire set of 29. This is the largest set in the world and was designed and tailored for St John’s Co-Cathedral in Valletta.

In April 2023, the co-cathedral decided to display them in the church, probably for the last time, since they are destined for the new museum now under construction.. The last time they were displayed in the church was in 1990, during Pope Saint John Paul II's visit.

The tapestries were to be brought down in July of the same year, and we were responsible for creating a digital model of the cathedral with the tapestries set up. I was tasked with leading this process, and within weeks, the team was formed, and the work began. Stargate Studios were chosen to carry out the digitisation and production aspect of this project.

St John’s Co-Cathedral receives approximately 3,000 visitors every day, making it Malta’s most popular tourist attraction. At the same time, it is an active place of worship, and Mass is celebrated daily. In other words, this limits scanning to late evenings and nights.

When your access is limited to evenings, you cannot afford to waste a moment. We meticulously planned and started immediately.

The scanning stage

We could access the space for scanning only from 7 pm onward, which also provided controlled lighting. We completed the entire acquisition over seven nights.

Three instruments were used for the scanning:

  1. DSLR: Canon EOS R5 cameras with 24mm lenses captured at native 8K, including from scaffolding and lifts for ceiling coverage.
  2. Drone: A DJI Mavic 3 Pro Cine drone provided elevated 5K perspectives at altitudes of 3 to 15 metres, with manually planned flight paths.
  3. LiDAR Scanner: A Faro Focus M70 delivered geometric structure through 60-minute scans, each producing over 100 million points.

Traditional photogrammetry requires circling objects from every direction, but that is impossible within such a space. A modified approach was therefore developed, beginning with wide shots, then moving incrementally closer and shooting chapels from outside their entrances to maintain alignment with the nave.

Stargate Studios carefully chose the range of instruments to maximise the processing stage. The sharp focus mattered more than a clean ISO in a dark building because it revealed fine detail for the photogrammetry algorithm to detect and align. Noise, or digital grain, can be removed later, but features cannot be reconstructed. The drone was manually piloted in key strategic areas of the cathedral to capture visual features at altitudes that were difficult for a human operator to reach. Finally, the LiDAR scanning provided the geometry within which the texture features captured by photography could be anchored.

Why gold leaf and photogrammetry are not friends

Photogrammetry fails on shiny surfaces that look too good. It assumes a point on a surface looks the same from every angle. Gold leaf, bronze and dark marble break that assumption, because their highlights move with the camera, so the software matches reflections instead of surfaces.

This was addressed by reducing contrast to flatten the images, because textures respond better to manual lighting in final applications and photogrammetry algorithms interpret colour variation as geometric change. Flattening dark imagery captured at ISO 12800 to 25600 introduces significant digital grain, particularly across the cathedral’s bronze, wood, and metal.

Adobe’s AI denoiser performed excellently but struggled with batches larger than 2,000 photos, so denoising all 99,000 images took approximately one month of continuous processing. The result preserves fine detail in the gilt work while producing much cleaner dark areas.

Where software stopped, and people started

LiDAR software merges scans on its own but cannot distinguish a 400-year-old column from a stack of chairs left out overnight or a scaffolding pole. This meant that all 43 scans were manually cleaned after capture. Separately, denoising had smoothed away some of the fine detail that the aligner depended on, so 108 control points, landmarks marked by hand in several photos so the software could tie them together, were entered manually. That is what produced 98.6% of images in a single aligned component.

Point cloud to mesh

We combined the three capture methods into one detailed model in four stages. First, there is a sparse point cloud with visible gaps, such as the altar painting. Then, a denser cloud is created by merging the remaining photographs and LiDAR data. The third step is an aligned, cleaned point cloud (without texture and colour), and the blue patches you see are just the back faces of the cropped section. This shouldn’t be confused with missing data. The fourth and last image is the finished, textured mesh.

The figure below shows the visual result of the process.

For scale, this one chapel section alone results in around a billion triangles. The full cathedral reconstruction sits somewhere between 25 and 30 billion.

What still resists the process

Not every surface was reconstructed cleanly, and the paper documents the failures as openly as the successes.

The tapestries

The twenty-nine Flemish tapestries, woven on Rubens’ designs, were photographed in 8K while hanging in the nave. They came out worse than anything else in the building. These tapestries are made out of fine wool and silk, with the largest ones measuring approximately 6x6m.

Hanging fabric moves with the building’s air circulation, and any movement between frames reads as error. The size of the tapestries, coupled with the time required to capture the images, meant there were enough small movements to distort the tapestries’ visuals in the first iteration of the 3D model, as shown below.

This was eventually fixed by photographing them flat during conservation and reprojecting onto smoothed meshes.

The dark curved marble

The funerary monument of Grand Master Zondadari, extremely dark, highly reflective and geometrically complex, pushed the pipeline to its limits. Visible artefacts remain on its curved marble edges despite LiDAR support. This demonstrates the technique’s limits with specular materials in low light.

The 3D asset

We merged the LiDAR point cloud with the photographic dataset. Of 93,066 images imported after quality review, 91,721 were successfully registered into a single aligned component, a 98.6% success rate. This produced 137.2 million tie points, the matched features that hold the model together, with a mean reprojection error of 0.26 pixels. In other words, each point lands on average about a quarter of a pixel from where the photos say it should be. Where automatic alignment failed, 108 manually placed control points bridged the gap. Total alignment time was roughly 24 production hours.

We also tested Gaussian splatting on one chapel, the Chapel of Germany. It kept the reflections on the gilding that the mesh loses, but the surfaces dissolve at close range, so we treat it as a companion to the mesh and not a replacement.

The LiDAR data required extensive cleanup before integration, since reflective surfaces degrade laser scan accuracy, introducing noise and, in some cases, false points below ground level. Across all 43 scans, mean point error came to 1.3 millimetres, tightening to 0.9 millimetres across the 28 scans covering the core nave.

The dataset was too large to process as a single unit. Each chapel was reconstructed individually before being combined by side; the altar section’s 33,000 photographs were split into roughly five processing chunks, and the completed point cloud was divided by room for mesh generation, with the altar alone split into nine overlapping pieces. Each room section produced approximately one billion triangles, for a project total of 25 to 30 billion triangles.

What is the archive for?

This project focused on scanning and creating a high-fidelity, millimetric scan of the cathedral. The completed reconstruction supports several applications documented in the paper.

These include disaster recovery documentation, providing a precise geometric record in the event of damage. When fire tore through Notre-Dame in 2019, laser scans made years earlier by the art historian Andrew Tallon became a reference for the restoration.

Conservation planning, allowing structural analysis without repeated physical access. Virtual tourism, opening global access to a space most visitors will never enter. As a dataset, this project also aims to strengthen scholarly research by enabling detailed examination of architectural and artistic elements at a level ordinary site visits don’t allow.

From a graphics and scientific perspective, the paper is equally clear about the model’s limitations. It captures the cathedral at a single point in time, geometry and colour, but not physical material properties like hardness or composition, and movable elements such as furniture and liturgical items were removed or repositioned during processing, so the model does not reflect the building’s day-to-day “in use” state. That gap between how a space looks and how it behaves is also an open problem in physical AI, where a machine needs to know what a surface is made of before it touches it. Periodic rescanning, as the paper notes, would be needed to track ongoing conservation change over time, and that in itself opens the dataset to further research opportunities.

Frequently asked questions

I posted about this paper and project on social media, and I received direct messages with specific questions. To make it easier to follow, I put together these FAQs:

What is photogrammetry? Photogrammetry is a technique for reconstructing three-dimensional geometry from overlapping two-dimensional photographs. Software identifies matching points across many images taken from different positions and triangulates their location in 3D space.

What is Gaussian splatting and how does it compare to photogrammetric meshes? Gaussian splatting represents a scene as a cloud of translucent 3D primitives rather than solid triangle geometry. It preserves reflections and view-dependent lighting effects that meshes struggle with, but loses geometric solidity at close viewing range. The two are best used as complementary representations.

How much data was captured? The processed dataset totalled approximately 2.18 TB, or roughly 22 MB per image after grading and denoising. All images were downscaled to 4K before alignment to keep the computational load manageable.

What software was used? Photogrammetric reconstruction was carried out in RealityCapture v1.5.1 (now RealityScan), which handled the alignment of the photographic dataset and its integration with the LiDAR point cloud. LiDAR registration and cleanup were done in Faro SCENE. Grain introduced during grading was removed with Adobe’s AI denoiser. The final meshes were subdivided for real-time use in Unreal Engine. Custom scripting handled proxy generation and systematic file naming across the 55 SD cards, and an automated plugin was used to split the altar mesh into overlapping pieces.

Can the public access the 3D model? Not yet, but the Foundation and our team are already working on the next phase.

The full SIGGRAPH 2026 paper

This post summarises the workflow at a high level.

The paper itself contains the complete methodology, full equipment specifications, all accuracy metrics and processing tables, and a discussion section with practical recommendations for heritage professionals planning similar large-scale digitisation projects.

Citation: Matthew Kenely, Mark Bugeja, Andre Grima, Peter Pullicino, Matthew Pullicino, Dylan Seychell, Large-Scale Photogrammetric Documentation of St John’s Co-Cathedral: A Workflow for Cultural Heritage Preservation, ACM SIGGRAPH 2026 Art Papers, Los Angeles, 19 to 23 July 2026. Published in the Proceedings of the ACM on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques (PACMCGIT).

His research applies computer vision and machine learning to the environment, through drones and geospatial AI, and to the information ecosystem, through news analysis and media transparency tools. title: The attack of the giant AI design slop monster: a survivor’s guide
text:
The attack of the giant AI design slop monster: a survivor’s guide

In 2026, AI has transformed UX design in unpredictable and scary ways

In September this year, I was once again speaking at City St George’s, University of London annual conference on Human-Computer Interaction Design, entitled “Rage Against the Machine”. This story expands upon my talk at that conference.

(Some images that accompany this story are AI-generated, including the dummy product example — as stated in the image descriptions. That’s kind of the whole point. The text, however, is 100% written with my own bare hands.)

AI for UX design (a dark twist)

Re-reading my writing on the subject of AI in UX from last year, I laugh at how outdated it appears today. While every prediction I had made last year has come true, we’re well into a territory I could not have anticipated in my wildest dreams.

Research-wise, most methods I used to rely on are not needed anymore: while robust human oversight and human interpretation remain crucial, structured prompting has given way to the model’s own intent inference; hallucinated user quotes are a thing of the past; and with correct templates, creating research reports is a breeze.

So instead, today I’d like to focus on AI for UX design. Last year, I still dismissed AI for design — it was sloppy and horrible and could not compete with me, a seasoned professional. This year… well. I went on a journey that took some dark turns. Thankfully, I emerged from it changed but victorious. For now.

Let’s start with some hypothetical scenarios.

A Product Manager, a developer and a UX designer walk into a bar. The barman asks, “So which one of you vibe codes, then?”

(Disclaimer: no product managers, developers or designers were harmed in the making of this episode. Any resemblance to actual persons, living or dead, is purely coincidental.)

Dubbed the word of the year by the Collins English Dictionary in 2025, vibe coding is, simply put, “the use of artificial intelligence prompted by natural language to assist with the writing of computer code.”

Scenario 1: The PM vibe codes

Your product manager has discovered Claude Code and, by giving it a couple of prompts, has turned every single idea from their backlog into a complete UI interface. They dump the lot on you during your weekly Teams call, prefaced with, “It’s just an idea. Don’t worry, you can draw it up properly later.”

Or worse, they don’t come to you at all but instead go straight to the senior leadership and table their “designs” — and the leadership is ecstatic. Finally, they don’t have to wait for weeks for you to draw things in Figma, or get it through your lengthy design systems approvals, or anything! Let’s go develop it tomorrow! In fact, it’s already developed, isn’t it, it’s a complete functional prototype, let’s ship it now!

And let’s say, the PM’s “design” looks like this — but no-one except you thinks it’s a problem:

You’ve lost control. What are you supposed to do now? Tidy up the PM’s slop, argue the toss, complain to the leadership?

Scenario 2: the developer vibe codes

Your dev team has been told by the leadership to use only AI-assisted code and they’ve embraced this brave new world. You might think: and so what? The developer codes, you don’t code. You don’t care what tools they use. Until they send you the cert environment link and instead of your beautiful Figma vision you see this:

“Why did it end up looking like this?” you ask your developer. Then you discover that they wholesale fed your Figma into Claude Code via MCP without any links to your design system library or any proper componetisation. Claude hallucinated some Frankensteinian approximations of your design, but if you squint, it sort of looks OK. Just don’t try to use the keyboard to check for focus states.

The developer and the business are ecstatic because it took them 3 days to produce that instead of the usual 3 months. Once again, the only one that sees the problem, is you.

Your existential crisis monster has landed. The monster is asking you, “Is UX even needed anymore? If you leave tomorrow, who even cares?”

Let’s look at some numbers.

This year, the tech industry has been shaken by AI like no other industry on Earth. 84% developers use AI for coding; product managers use it for absolutely everything, from brainstorming to senior leadership presentations. And PMs frequently trample the territory previously occupied by UX researchers and designers — because they can. For them, it’s now easier than ever, a mere prompt away.

UX designers, on the other hand, are behind. Perfectionism prevented us from experimenting with early AI design tools because these were so terrible, barely good enough for ideation. But UX designers today no longer have the luxury of pixel pushing — everyone else is ahead. Meanwhile, AI design tools are improving by the day.

Scenario 3: you fix what you can — and vibe code your own slop

So, as the only one who cares about UX/UI, you’re going to fix it. How?

1. Fix things with the PM

PROBLEM: solutionising — “It’s just an idea”.
FIX: revert back to user problem.
Make your PM state what user problems they are solving, help them determine what user evidence there is already. Fill the gaps with new user research.

PROBLEM: AI design slop.
FIX: “skeleton UI”.
Define the minimum UI rules to AI-ideate within. Everyone must follow them — whether PM or UX.

PROBLEM: you’re too slow.
FIX: make your own AI slop, fast.
You can’t win against a machine gun with a bow & arrow, so get armed with the same tools and slop away, knowing that your slop will be better than the PM’s slop.

You have the designer’s eye. You also have the researcher’s eye. While the PM may not have thought of how user research is represented, how to avoid pointless or weird UI, how to ensure visual consistency and design system rigour, you will have thought of all these things. As you vibe code like your life depends on it, knowing that your sloppy design will be a functional approximation to the perfect Platonic form you have in your head.

Feed your Claude app the body of your user research, feed it your “skeleton UI”, describe what to build in detail, link it to your design system (more on this later), give it the required accessibility standards to follow, ask it to generate realistic dummy content (which you should check with a human subject-matter expert), provide it with “done when” criteria. Press the button. Get yourself a coffee while Claude does its thing.

2. Fix things with the developers

PROBLEM: frontend quality deteriorates due to AI-assisted coding.
FIX: define your “minimum bar”.
Decide what your lowest acceptable UI quality looks like, spell out WCAG compliance, define componetisation rules the developer should follow.

PROBLEM: developer has low frontend knowledge and can’t spot AI mishaps.
FIX: institute QA checks of their work.
If any “minumum bar” items don’t make it to product release, insist on cleanup afterwards.

PROBLEM: “Don’t Stop Me Now” — the developer just can’t get enough of AI speed.
FIX: work fast and be prepared to compromise.
Make your QA checks rapid and responsive. You won’t win by being a perfectionist — pick your battles.

How to keep the AI design slop monster under control

So you’ve managed to stave off your existential crises with your team and you’re now happily AI-designing/vibe coding. Let’s take a look at how that can be done better.

I’ve used a handful of different AI design tools, many others are out there, but I suspect the principles of working with all of them are much the same.

Principle 1. Create your user research guardrails.

I cannot overstate this: always start from the user. Feed the AI tool the research findings (best as structured reports rather than raw data, as these are more machine readable). Give the AI tool the full context and test its understanding of the context before progressing.

Principle 2. Create your design guardrails.

Without these rigorous guardrails, your AI tool will ride you instead of you riding it. Fixing AI design errors can be frustrating and can quickly eat into your token allowance for the month.

This is what I meant earlier when talking about “setting up skeleton UI”. It includes components but also templates, patterns, interaction rules, accessibility — the whole UX design microcosm.

These guardrails can be set at multiple levels of sophistication, starting from simply giving the AI tool a URL link of a design system. The next step could be Figma MCP (if using Figma as a base) to get your Figma specs and your AI tool to talk to each other. Then, Code Connect can help link your Figma components with your company’s GitHub component library, preventing the AI tool from hallucinating components from scratch. You might jump between Figma and an AI-generated prototype before arriving at your perfect design solution.

The advantage of AI prototyping is that it is vastly faster than traditional design, allowing you to explore multiple options before you’ve finished that coffee of yours. Another great advantage is that it can be made to behave like a live product — brilliant for user testing.

Principle 3. Respect safety and security.

Safety and security should not be an afterthought. AI tools, especially ones capable of accessing your computer and your company’s systems (such as Claude and Codex apps), are increasingly powerful and thus dangerous. From scandalous incidents like the agentic hacking of Hugging Face, to more mundane ones where Claude Code wiped 116GB of personal data — these stories abound.

You must at least do this: when giving the AI tool access to your files, confine it to one local folder only; keep backups of your precious data in locations that AI has no access to; monitor what permissions you are giving to the tool during each session.

This might be a no-brainer in 2026, but be aware that free and low-tier personal subscriptions allow AI tools to scrape your or your company’s data. Only share IP with the tool that you know is safe — for example, because your company has an enterprise subscription to it.

What happens next?

There are already AI-assisted UX design methods that bypass Figma altogether. If your component and pattern library is mature, once you connect it directly to Claude (for example, via a prototype environment linked to GitHub), in theory, there’s nothing stopping you from just designing in Claude. Make your prototype shareable online via Claude Artifacts (as of this month, it replaces Claude Design) and your frontend engineer might even be able to reuse your AI-generated code.

It might even be that over time, boundaries between UX design and frontend will blur — some UX designers already contribute to frontend code alongside developers, via AI tools.

Spec-Driven Development is another relatively new kid on the block. Behind it is the promise that, if all the essential information (including your UX rules for research, design, accessibility and whatnot) is fed to the AI tool in a specific, machine-readable format, it can produce a complete product in one hit, with no slop to clean up. This approach shows promise — albeit so far, it is not yet the unicorn that everyone has been hoping for (but that is a subject for another story).

Epilogue: the many Ailments

In the words of a colleague, “A month is a 100 years in AI time”. Who knows what I will be writing about a year on. Today, I am certainly suffering from the “UpSkill Sisyphus” ailment, aptly described by Information is Beautiful. I confess that I have even wondered whether AI might soon take my job.

I remain an optimist, however. Which user problems deserve solving? Who has the overall UI vision? Who can read between the lines to establish the future UX strategy? For as long as humans need digital products, UX processes — whether AI-powered or not — will need human input.

For now, the AI monster is somewhat tamed… As for the rest, the future will show!

title: Prototypes have always been the most effective specification-especially with AI
text:
Prototypes have always been the most effective specification-especially with AI

Prototypes have always been the most effective specification—especially with AI

When building a working version costs an afternoon, the artifact that used to precede the work now falls out of it instead.

Somebody on your team has a working version of the feature, and the requirements review is still three days out. They built it between meetings and did not mention it, because the plan said write the requirements, get sign-off, then build.

Then it lands in Slack and the room changes.

Three open questions in the document answer themselves once you can click the thing, and two more turn out to be the wrong ones.

Most teams would call that working backwards.

I have watched it often enough to stop calling it a failure, because the document written afterward beats the one that would have come first.

Who built it matters less now and we have to accept that.

That somebody might be a product manager, a designer, or an engineer, and all three can do it in an afternoon.

We all have to get comfortable with anyone producing the prototype, because that is what this new world has enabled, and there is no way to stop it.

The specification did not become useless when building got cheap. It changed position in the sequence, which gave it a new job: from a prediction about a system nobody had touched to a record of what building it settled.

Trace Why Specifications Exist

The specification is a cost artifact. It exists because building was expensive and writing about it was cheap, so teams bought certainty in the cheap medium before spending in the expensive one. The rituals follow from that trade: the sign-off, the change request, the version number on the cover page.

I once wrote a 1,200-page specification, and it was a waste of my time.

Writing was never a description of the system. It was the cheapest available simulation of building one.

In his 1986 essay No Silver Bullet, Fred Brooks argued that the hardest part of building software is deciding what to build. In his view, clients do not know what they want until they have seen a version running.

His fix was rapid prototyping at a moment when prototyping still cost real money, so most teams nodded and kept writing requirements.

The person writing them holds a model of the system in their head and cannot un-know it, which my reference site files under the Curse of Knowledge. I have run rapid prototyping with my own teams at multiple companies, and it has been very, very effective.

A prototype gets that model out of one head and onto a screen everyone can test.

Prototype Before the Review

What changed is not the argument, it is the price of the alternative.

Eric Ries gave the idea a cycle in 2011 with The Lean Startup: build, measure, learn, and repeat. He and Brooks both assumed building was the slow step.

UX Tools surveyed 1,478 self-selected designers for State of Prototyping: Spring 2026, and 59.1 percent had built their own tool, application, or utility with artificial intelligence in the previous six months. That number describes what one designer can put in front of a room by Thursday.

A prototype does not win arguments. It ends them, by turning a disagreement about a hypothetical into an observation about a thing.

The questions a requirements document handles worst, like behavior under load or the fourth step of a flow, are cheap to answer and costly to guess. Enterprise software is a good place to start iterating, because most of its design patterns are solved.

Tables, filters, forms, approvals, and permissions have been worked over for decades, and systems like Carbon, which calls itself an “enterprise-ready, open-source design system,” write them down as components.

A prototype built from those parts looks credible on the first afternoon, which saves the iteration for the workflow no library covers.

Run Research Every Week

A working version also changes what research is for. Discovery used to be a phase: interviews before the requirements, a study before launch, and a long quiet stretch between. When a team can build something new every few days, each build raises a question nobody had last week, and a study that wrapped in March cannot answer it.

Discovery stops being a phase you finish. It is always on, because every build asks a new question.

Teresa Torres has argued for that cadence. Her definition of continuous discovery calls for “weekly touch points with customers by the team building the product,” run in pursuit of a desired outcome.

Cheap prototypes give those sessions something to react to instead of a description to imagine.

Stakeholders reading requirements argue about what a user would do, while participants in front of a prototype simply do it. The researcher’s job shifts from running a study to keeping that loop honest: choosing which build meets which people, and saying out loud when the team is mostly testing its own enthusiasm.

Use the RITE Method

Usability testing went through this inversion once already. In 2002, Michael Medlock and colleagues at Microsoft described Rapid Iterative Testing and Evaluation in Using the RITE method to improve products; a definition and a case study.

A classic study runs every participant, then writes a report. RITE changes the interface “as soon as a problem is identified and a solution is clear,” sometimes after a single participant.

RITE stopped waiting for the full study, the way cheap builds now stop waiting for the full specification.

On the Age of Empires II tutorial, the team changed the design after six of its first ten participants and fixed 30 of the 31 problems it found.

One condition carried the method: the development team’s decision makers had to take part, which the paper calls “more than a commitment to attend and review.” That is the room this article keeps describing, with the user finally in it.

Small samples were never the weak point: Jakob Nielsen argued in 2000’s Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users that five participants surface roughly 85 percent of usability problems, a figure researchers still debate. Put a build in front of five people on Monday, fix it between sessions, and the specification you write Friday describes behavior you watched.

Write the Specification Last

So write the specification, and write it second. While the team iterates, the prototype is the working document: the thing people edit, review, and point at.

It is also the source of truth.

When the prototype and a paragraph disagree, the prototype wins, because it is the one somebody tested.

The specification becomes the account of how the prototype got that way, and its author has stopped guessing. It records which approach was tried, what broke, and why the surviving option won. That is closer to what Jeff Jeff Gothelf and Josh Seiden asked for in Lean UX, which steers teams toward the product experience rather than deliverables.

More people can build that working version than two years ago. Figma’s 2026 AI Report, drawn from 8,403 survey responses, found the share of designers participating in development doubled to 41 percent, while developers doing design work rose from 44 to 60 percent. As that line thins, the prototype stops belonging to one role and becomes the team’s shared working document.

A specification written before the build is a forecast. One written after is a record of decisions somebody already tested.

Writing the account no longer starts from a blank page either. Cursor’s Generating Documentation with Cursor says it “reads your code and generates documentation that reflects what the code does,” design documents and architecture overviews included.

Claude Code’s Common workflows guide suggests asking it to “explain the main architecture patterns used here” and “what are the key data models?” The specification can come out of the same tool that built the prototype, with a person editing in the decisions the code cannot explain.

For features built on a model, evals are the new specification: example inputs paired with the outputs the team expects, run every time the system changes. Dianne Penn, who leads product for Anthropic’s research teams, described the eval-driven development loop on Lenny’s Podcast in July 2026.

The New Stack reported in The 24-hour experiment that helped Anthropic find its identity that her team builds about 30 to 40 representative examples for each major feature. A paragraph can say what good looks like, but an eval checks it on every build.

Review the Prototype’s Defaults

Here the inversion gets costly, and enthusiasm makes it harder to see. The research nonprofit METR explained in We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design why it was redesigning its 2025 productivity study.

Between 30 and 50 percent of surveyed developers declined to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without artificial intelligence. The measurement broke on the affection of the people being measured.

The prototype answers the question you asked it. It also quietly answers about forty you did not.

Failure paths, blank screens, the data model, the accessibility of a control grabbed from a library: all decided, none discussed. The pattern I keep running into is the borrowed component nobody logged as a choice, a date picker or a modal in production because it arrived inside a demonstration everyone liked.

Starting from solved patterns is right; starting from them without logging which ones is how they ship unexamined. My Automation Bias entry explains the pull: a produced answer feels more settled than a proposed one. In regulated work, the document is still the artifact of record.

Write for Coding Agents

The build-first and specification-first camps look like rivals, but they mostly describe the same loop from opposite ends. In September 2025, GitHub released Spec Kit, described in Spec-driven development with AI: Get started with a new open source toolkit.

It starts with a specification that becomes the source of truth an agent uses to generate, test, and validate code. That sounds like requirements-first work until you ask who the document is for.

Both camps are right, because they are describing two different documents for two different readers.

An approver wanted confidence. An agent needs constraints: the boundary conditions, the naming rules, the thing you must never do to the billing table. You cannot write those precisely from imagination; you write them from the version you built, watched fail, and corrected.

Those constraints then move into the agent harness, the instruction files, permissions, hooks, and tests around the model, where the instructions state the rules and the rest enforce them. The harness becomes the guardrail.

GitHub’s study of more than 2,500 repositories, How to write a great agents.md: Lessons from over 2,500 repositories, found most agent files fail by being too vague and advises adding detail as the agent makes mistakes. That is writing from the build under another name. The agent’s source of truth sits downstream of the team’s: the prototype writes the specification, and that specification briefs the next build.

Discard the First Prototype

Brooks had a second line. In The Mythical Man-Month, he told managers to “plan to throw one away; you will, anyhow.” Teams that build first have to take that advice literally, and most do not.

The afternoon prototype gets a real URL, then a real user, then a ticket to harden it, and nobody ever decides it became the product if expectations are set well.

Developers already feel what code that almost works costs them.

Stack Overflow surveyed more than 49,000 developers for Developers remain willing but reluctant to use AI: The 2025 Developer Survey results are here, and 45 percent named solutions that are almost right as their top frustration. Two-thirds said they spend more time fixing that kind of code.

A prototype is supposed to be almost right.

Production is not, and the specification is where a team writes down which of the two it is holding.

Conclusion

None of this makes documentation optional. It moves the document to the point in the sequence where it can be accurate, which is after somebody has touched the thing it describes. It also gives research something new to put in front of users every week, which no document offers.

The requirements document was always a forecast dressed as a contract, and forecasts were the best instrument available while building stayed costly. That has stopped being true for a widening slice of work, and the practice around it has not caught up.

What I would watch on your team is the gap between the written schedule and the observed behavior. The calendar still says specification review on Tuesday. The Slack thread says somebody built it Sunday night. When those two facts sit side by side and nobody remarks on it, your process is describing a cost structure that no longer exists.

I would not sell the new order as a method, and I would distrust anyone who does. Building first smuggles in decisions nobody chose, and that cost is real. I would rather audit a working thing than defend a confident paragraph about a problem that turned out not to exist.

Reorder Your Next Feature

  • Build and test the smallest version. One screen built from components your design system already solved, shown to five users before anyone books the review. Fix between sessions, then put a new build in front of new people every week.
  • Write from the build. Let your coding tool draft the specification from the prototype, then add the reasoning it leaves out. When the prototype and the document disagree, fix the document. Replace every sentence beginning “the system shall” with one naming the attempt, the failure, and the option left standing. If you could not defend a line in a live demonstration, it is still a forecast and goes in the open column.
  • Audit the silent defaults. Walk the empty fields, the error messages, and every borrowed component; twenty minutes catches most of what the demonstration hid.
  • Write for the executor. A coding agent follows instructions literally and fills silence with invention, so name constraints and prohibitions, not intentions. Move the ones that matter into the harness, where a hook or a test enforces them, and for model-driven features, let the eval set serve as the specification.

title: Send the Firefighters to the Fires
text:
Send the Firefighters to the Fires

Send the firefighters to the fires

Enterprise software keeps forgetting a century of good advice about what deserves our attention.

If a user’s job is to fix what’s broken, the screen should show what’s broken first. Sounds pretty obvious. It’s also not new. Frederick Taylor argued for it in 1903. Xerox PARC designed for it in the ’90s. Industrial control rooms wrote it into a standard. Yet enterprise software keeps forgetting this.

Imagine a fire department that dispatches trucks in the order houses were built. Or by date last renovated. Every house gets a visit eventually, and some of them happen to be on fire. That’s pretty absurd, right? Yet I’ve seen the equivalent more times than I care to remember.

A lot of enterprise work boils down to one job: here’s a collection of things, some of them have problems, go fix the problems. Devices out of compliance. Certificates about to expire. Invoices that failed to reconcile. Tickets breaching SLA. The KPI is simply “issues resolved.”

The UI has one job: get the user to the fires and hand them the hose.

So how did we forget? Not because the ideas are hard. Enterprise software just has a habit of designing for everyone except the person actually using it. It’s designing for the buyer in the demo, for the team racing to ship, for the data model that sorts things for free. None of them pay for it. But the user does, every shift, one scroll at a time.

Start with the job

Clayton Christensen had a simple idea: people don’t buy products for their features. They hire them to get a job done. It’s now known as Jobs to Be Done, or JTBD (Christensen et al., 2016; open-access overview). In enterprise triage, the job is about as plain as it gets: fix what’s broken. Finding it should be the product’s job.

So why do so many screens ignore this? Here’s the pattern I see over and over again. A screen lists 400 objects, and twelve need attention. They’re scattered somewhere between page 3 and page 17. It’s Where’s Waldo, except Waldo is a production outage.

Sometimes there’s a status column. Maybe a small red pill, sitting politely in column six of a list sorted by anything but what matters. A human can work out which items are broken. But the interface is acting obtuse and unhelpful.

Consider the following twenty services. I’ll keep coming back to them.

Before: 20 rows, sorted by last updated, every column visible

After: focus on the fires

In the first table, the two critical services sit in rows sixteen and nineteen, and nothing calls them critical. You have to cross-reference Health and Tier yourself: search-index is only Degraded, but it’s Tier 1; mail-relay is Failing, but it’s Tier 3. Meanwhile, Uptime reads 99.92% for payments-gw, which is failing right now. The fires-first view does that math for you. Same data, different job.

Now imagine hearing that table instead. If the headers are marked up properly, a screen reader announces which column you’re in as you move through it (W3C, F91). So a screen reader user can walk down the Health column one cell at a time. That’s still twenty announcements to find six problems, plus a hop to the Tier column for each one. And that’s the best case: many enterprise data grids are built from divs, virtualized, or paginated, and those shortcuts break. Many enterprises don’t hire people who can build accessible tables (Brad Frost calls them front-of-the-front-end developers), but that’s another story. For every column of noise we leave in, someone has to sit through it.

None of this is malicious. Nobody in the review said “hey, let’s bury the critical issues!” The order happened by default, because nobody dug into the JTBD.

The table as a design cop-out

Bad sort order is an outcome of enterprise’s unfortunate love affair with the table as a magic bullet.

The reasoning goes: we don’t know exactly what users want, so let’s give them all the data and let them search, filter, and sort. It sounds like giving users control. In reality, it’s an abdication.

Those are tools for exploring and hunting: browsing to see what’s there, or tracking down something you know exists. But when they become the main interface for task work, the product team has handed its job to the user. Every session, someone sorts by health, scrolls past the Passing rows, cross-checks the tier, and finds payments-gw. Again. Multiply that by every user, every day. That’s triage the product could have done once.

At some point, some smarty-pants will suggest saved filters: let users build and save their own “To-dos” view (health is failing, sorted by tier). Problem solved, right? Not quite! That’s a workaround stacked on the cop-out. Users end up designing the default screen for you because you shipped the wrong one.

Why smart teams keep doing this

To be fair, the people shipping these screens aren’t careless. The forces pushing them toward the table are real, and a lot of them trace back to one thing: in sales-led enterprise software, the buyer isn’t the user.

Jason Lemkin said it bluntly back in 2012: “you, the end user, aren’t the customer for most true enterprise software” (Lemkin, SaaStr). A year later, Martin Eriksson made the same distinction for product managers: “the user and the purchaser are different people with different needs” (Eriksson, Mind the Product).

The buyer’s worst case is a boring demo. The user’s worst case is an outage with their name on it. Guess who the screen gets designed for. Not every lazy sort comes from sales, but a sales-led motion makes lazy sorts easier to ship and harder to undo.

Defaults feel safe. Every record has a created_at and an updated_at, so sorting by them is free. “Severity” doesn’t exist until someone designs it. Meanwhile, stakeholders worry that if healthy items aren’t visible, users will assume they’re missing, and on an RFP checklist, a hidden column might as well not exist. So everything stays on screen.

Nobody talks to each other. Taiichi Ohno’s 5 Whys only works if you can reach the person with the answer. In enterprise, there are too many layers between the people willing to ask and the people able to answer. The only two people reliably talking are the salesperson and the buyer. The salesperson is paid for the close, and asking why five times only gets in the way. Conway’s law predicts the result: systems mirror how their makers communicate. A neutral sort is what that silence looks like on screen.

“Ask ‘why’ five times about every matter.”
 — Taiichi Ohno, Toyota

Dashboards are built for the demo. People love dashboards that look like command centers in movies. Walls of screens! Scrolling numbers! Blinking maps! Stephen Few was criticizing exactly this two decades ago, arguing that dashboards should support real-time situation awareness for decision making, not impress the room (Few, 2007; Information Dashboard Design, 2006). Density still wins sales calls, which is the sales motion showing up in the UI. Developers and PMs love it too: every widget and column is a feature someone built.

Tables are cheap and familiar. Every component library ships one, and every IC has built a dozen, so it’s what everyone reaches for first. Inline editing is one prop away, so someone will eventually float turning every cell into a form field. Cheap to build, expensive to use.

Notice what these have in common? Each one optimizes for the team’s comfort or the buyer’s first impression, not the user’s job. The table can never be wrong, because it never commits to anything.

Tables aren’t the enemy

To be clear, I’m not anti-table. Reporting, analysis, and bulk admin are table work. User questions can change week to week, and pinning them down takes the kind of conversations we’ve already seen are rare. Designing for that is tough, so a flexible table is an honest answer.

The line I draw is this: open-ended questions need flexible tables. Known jobs need opinionated ones.

Yet sometimes the best table is the one you don’t build! Think about what people actually do with a big table, and where that work belongs:

  • Slice and pivot? Let them export to (or integrate with) the BI tools they already know.
  • Report up to leadership? Send a scheduled summary, not a screenshot of 400 rows.
  • Reconcile against another system? That’s an integration or an API. Please don’t subject a human being to comparing two systems row by row.
  • Hand evidence to auditors? Send an export instead of buying them a seat, which only gets them a login they’ll barely use, to a worse BI tool.

Excel, Tableau, and Power BI are established, they’re good at analysis, and your users already know them. Your product doesn’t need to compete. Just keep the fires list live and in-app.

So the question isn’t table or no table. It’s what goes in it, and in what order. If you can write the user’s job in one sentence, and “resolve the issues” is that sentence, you know enough to decide: fires first, ranked by severity, healthy rows summarized. A table sorted by last updated with every row at equal weight is just an inventory. It tells users what exists, not what needs their attention.

Management by exception, a century later

One of my core design principles fits in four words: no news is good news. I didn’t invent it. In 1903, Frederick Taylor called it the exception principle: a manager shouldn’t be swamped with every report, only with what deviates from the standard (Taylor, Shop Management).

“The manager should receive only condensed, summarized, and invariably comparative reports.”
 — Frederick Winslow Taylor, Shop Management (1903)

Swap “manager” for “user” and it’s a design brief. There’s no reason to emphasize what’s working. Working is the expected state; it’s what the customer pays for. But there’s every reason to emphasize what isn’t, because that’s the only part that needs a human.

Every pixel that gives a healthy object the same weight as a broken one is friction against the KPI. If the metric is issues resolved, a screen that hides issues isn’t neutral. It’s working against the business. And noise isn’t just visual. For a screen reader user, it’s time.

So design as if the user’s job performance depends on your decisions. Because it does! When issues slip through the cracks, nobody blames the designer who picked the default sort. They blame the user who didn’t spot payments-gw in time. They inherit our defaults, our clutter, and our shallow thinking, and they’re the ones who get penalized for it.

That’s the bar. It’s not “does it follow the design system” or “did stakeholders sign off.” It’s “does this make the person using it better at their job?”

What control rooms already know

Ironically, real control rooms don’t look like the movies. In refineries and power plants, operator screens are guided by the ISA-101 standard for industrial interfaces (ISA, 2015), which builds on the high-performance HMI work of Bill Hollifield and colleagues (The High Performance HMI Handbook). Normal operation stays gray and calm. Color is saved for when something’s wrong.

https://medium.com/media/3a2b27bedfc398539b462d0027464e6c/href

The unsexy truth is that sometimes, that’s all a dashboard needs to be: a prioritized list of what’s on fire and the means to put it out, not a bunch of widgets fighting for the user’s attention. Many may not like it, but that’s what peak performance looks like. Operators knew it long before enterprise SaaS did.

Silence has to be earned

Here’s a fair objection: users need reassurance. If I only show problems, how does anybody know the rest is fine?

Sure, Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic covers it. Systems should keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time (Harley, NN/g). No news is only good news if the silence is trustworthy. An empty screen could mean everything is healthy, or that the sync broke an hour ago. If users can’t tell the difference, they’ll go back to scanning the full table.

So design the quiet state as deliberately as the loud one. Don’t list the healthy items. Summarize them with confidence.

Just a count, a timestamp, and a way to dig deeper. You’re still reporting the good news. You’re just not giving it top billing.

Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown described this balance in 1995 as calm technology: information that sits in the periphery of our attention and moves to the center only when it matters (Weiser and Brown, 1995). In their words, the periphery is “informing without overburdening.” That’s the quiet state. It gives users permission to stop looking. Giving users their time back might be the most underrated thing an enterprise tool can offer.

What fires-first actually looks like

A fires-first approach isn’t just the same table with a different sort. Here’s what separates it, with credit where it’s due.

  • Severity, not just status. A small fire next to a gas station beats a big one in an empty lot. An expired certificate on payments-gw outranks one on a test server, even if both say “Failing.” Health tells you what broke. Tier tells you how much it matters. Severity needs both. Remember that severity doesn’t exist until someone designs it? This is what designing it looks like.
  • Urgency and importance are separate axes. The idea is usually traced to a 1954 Eisenhower speech, and Stephen Covey, A. Roger Merrill, and Rebecca Merrill turned it into four quadrants in First Things First (Hoang, Rework). Plot issues on that matrix, and users can make meaningful choices about what to fix now, schedule, delegate, or snooze.
  • Lead straight into investigation. Fires seldom have a one-click fix. The real job is usually figuring out what went wrong, so each item should invite investigation.
  • Notify, so nobody has to watch. People have better things to do than babysit your app. When payments-gw catches fire, tell the person who can fix it, wherever they already work: email, Slack, Teams. The fires list is where they go to act, not where they sit and wait.
  • Restraint on alerts. Healthcare has studied the opposite failure for years. When clinicians are flooded with warnings, they become desensitized and start overriding the critical ones along with the trivial ones (AHRQ PSNet, “Alert Fatigue”). If 300 of 400 items say “Warning,” your users will do the same. A severity model that can’t say “this doesn’t matter now” isn’t a severity model.
  • Let users snooze. Some fires can’t be fought today: a vendor hasn’t replied, or the fix needs a maintenance window. Snoozing dials down the noise without pretending the issue is solved, and it comes back on schedule.
  • Resolution is visible. When a fire goes out, it leaves the list and the count drops. That feedback loop makes the KPI real to the person doing the work.
  • Everything is still one click away. The full table, healthy rows included, for the audit, the export, and the curious.
“I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important.”
— Dwight D. Eisenhower, quoting J. Roscoe Miller, 1954

The top-right quadrant leads the fires list. Everything else still has a home.

Not sure where to start? Watch how users triage today: what they sort by, what they scroll past, what they export. Your users have already mentally drafted the spec.

Dispatch, not census

A census counts everyone equally. That’s its job. A dispatch center decides who needs help first and sends people there.

Most enterprise dashboards are built like a census: complete, neutral, accurate. And no help to someone whose job is putting out the fires.

Taylor got there in 1903. Weiser and Brown in 1995. Few in 2006. The ISA-101 committee in 2015. Same direction, a century apart. The knowledge isn’t missing. What’s missing is defining what “on fire” means, ranking it, designing the quiet state, and wiring up the notifications.

Do the extra work so your users don’t have to. That’s the job.

Further reading

In order of appearance:

  • Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, and David S. Duncan, “Know Your Customers’ ‘Jobs to Be Done,’” Harvard Business Review, September 2016. Open-access overview: Kelsey Miller, “The Jobs to Be Done Framework Explained & Real-World Examples,” Harvard Business School Online, 2020 (updated 2026)
  • W3C, “F91: Failure of Success Criterion 1.3.1 for not correctly marking up table headers,” WCAG 2.2 Techniques
  • Brad Frost, “Front-of-the-front-end and back-of-the-front-end web development,” bradfrost.com, 2021
  • Jason Lemkin, “Real Ent Software Don’t Need No Stinkin’ UI/UX,” SaaStr, 2012
  • Martin Eriksson, “Consumer vs Enterprise Product Management,” Mind the Product, 2013
  • Melvin E. Conway, “How Do Committees Invent?” Datamation, April 1968. Overview: “Conway’s law,” Wikipedia
  • Taiichi Ohno, Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production, Productivity Press, 1988. Overview: “Five whys,” Wikipedia
  • Stephen Few, “Dashboard Design for Real-Time Situation Awareness,” Perceptual Edge, 2007; and Information Dashboard Design, O’Reilly, 2006
  • Frederick Winslow Taylor, Shop Management (1903). Context: Management by exception, Rework
  • International Society of Automation, ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015, Human Machine Interfaces for Process Automation Systems, 2015
  • Bill Hollifield, Dana Oliver, Ian Nimmo, and Eddie Habibi, The High Performance HMI Handbook, PAS, 2008
  • Aurora Harley, “Visibility of System Status (Usability Heuristic #1),” Nielsen Norman Group, 2018
  • Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown, “Designing Calm Technology,” Xerox PARC, 1995
  • Victor Hoang, “The History of the Eisenhower Matrix: From a 1954 Remark to Covey’s Four Quadrants,” Rework, 2026
  • Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, “Alert Fatigue,” PSNet, 2019 (reviewed 2024)
